## The positioning segment


### GPS or GNSS?

::: {.incremental}
- Main \acr{GNSS} constellations:

    - \acr{GPS} (USA) [1970’s – 1990’s]{.fragment .fade-in}
    - \acr{GLONASS} (Russia) [980’s – 1996 (<8 sats) – 2007 (24 sats)]{.fragment .fade-in}
    - Galileo (Europe) [2002 (approved) – 2019 (\acr{FOC})]{.fragment .fade-in}
    - \acr{INRSS} (India) [2006 (approved) – 2018 (regional)]{.fragment .fade-in}
    - Beidou (China) [2000 – 2003 (experimental) – 2012 (regional) – 2020 (global)]{.fragment .fade-in}
:::

::: {.incremental}
- *Augmentation* systems:
    - \acr{WAAS} (USA) 1990’s – 2003 (FOC)
    - \acr{EGNOS} (Europe) 2001 – 2011 (FOC)
    - \acr{MSAS} (Japan) 2007
    - \acr{GAGAN} (India) 2013
    - \acr{SDCM} (Russia) 2015
:::

### Augmentation systems: satellite

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.incremental}
- Coverage area at the level of a continent/country
- Safety critical system designed to augment one or several \acr{GNSS}
- Corrections relayed by a \acr{GEO} satellite
- Has several segments like main \acr{GNSS}
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![source: Navipedia (ESA)](assets/figures/SBAS_overview.png)
:::

:::

### Augmentation systems: satellite

![source: Navipedia (ESA)](assets/figures/sbas_service_areas.png)


### Augmentation systems: regional

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.incremental}
- *Differential* GPS for aviation with multiple antennas and receivers (3 to 4)
- Cross checking of measurements from different receivers
- Averaging mitigates uncorrelated errors
- Redundancy of hardware
- Integrity data provided to user locally using radio link
- Coverage of local area(~20 km)
- Used for airports as alternative to \acr{ILS}
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](assets/figures/gbas_overview.png)
:::

:::


### European GNSS

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
- \acr{EGNOS}:
  - "Overlay" system that *augments* \acr{GPS} and \acr{GLONASS}
  - European coverage
  - Three services: \acr{OS}, \acr{SoL}, and \acr{EDAS}
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](assets/figures/EGNOS_Logo_pillars.jpg)
:::
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
- Galileo
  - Autonomous infrastructure
  - Global coverage
  - Steadily improving performance
  - Additional added value services besides positioning
  - Complex and distributed infrastructure built through cooperation among European member states
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](assets/figures/Galileo_logo_pillars.jpg)
:::
:::

### European GNSS: Why Galileo?

Europe's technological sovereignty in positioning

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- First GNSS designed and operated under **civil control**
- As of 2008, financed entirely by EU and managed by the \acr{EC}
- Provides Europe independence from other GNSS, greater robustness, and additional positioning services
- Interoperability with other GNSS for increased accuracy and availability
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](assets/figures/galileo_sat.jpg)
:::
:::

### Galileo stakeholders

![source: chatGPT](assets/figures/galileo_stakeholders.svg)

### Galileo services


| Service | Description | Accuracy / Features | Target Users |
|---|---|---|---|
| OS – Open Service | Free and open to everyone | Meters | General users (navigation, smartphones, GPS apps) |
| HAS – High Accuracy Service | Real-time corrections | Centimeters | Precision agriculture, drones, engineering, transport |
| OS – Navigation Message Authentication | Authentication of navigation messages | N/A | All users, especially critical applications |
| SAR – Search and Rescue | Location of distress beacons (Cospas-Sarsat) + Return Link Service | Rapid localization | Emergency situations, people in distress at sea/mountains/aviation |
| PRS – Public Regulated Service | Encrypted and robust signal | High, even in adverse conditions | Governments, military, police, civil protection |

### Using the stars: North hemisphere


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
Finding your way with stars:

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
::: {.incremental}
1. Locate the **Big Dipper** constellation
2. Find the **pointer stars** (Dubhe and Merak) at the end of the Big Dipper's bowl
3. Draw a line from these stars to locate the North Star (Polaris), about **5 times** the distance between Dubhe and Merak
4. Polaris is located almost directly above the North Pole, so it indicates true north
:::

### Inertial navigation



::: {.columns}

::: {.column}


- With electronic engineering appearing in the 20th century, \acr{INS} were developed
- Two main observations:
  - acceleration (accelerometers)
  - angular velocity (gyroscopes)
- Types of \acr{INS}:
  - Mechanical \acr{INS} (gyroscopes and accelerometers)
  - Optical \acr{INS} (ring laser gyroscopes and fiber optic gyroscopes)
  - MEMS \acr{INS} (microelectromechanical systems)


:::

::: {.column}



![](assets/figures/ins.png)


:::

:::


### Hyperbolic navigation


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
- With the appearance of radio technology, terrestrial hyperbolic navigation systems were developed in the 20th century
  - \acr{LORAN} (US, 1940s)
  - Decca (UK, 1940s)
  - Omega (US, 1970s, global coverage)
- Hyperbolic navigation systems are based on the measurement of the difference in time of arrival (\acr{TDoA}) of radio signals from two or more transmitters
:::

::: {.column}
![source: Wikipedia](assets/figures/Accuracy_of_Navigation_Systems.svg)
:::

:::

### Satellite positioning: Transit



::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

- Military origins (early 1960s): U.S. Navy’s, DARPA and J. H. Applied Physics Lab.
- Operation: 2 signals UHF (300 MHz – 3 GHz)
  - Satellite orbit computation
  - Positioning based on **Doppler** effect
- Drawbacks:
  - Complex localization algorithm (successive adjustments and updates)
  - Low availability in some zones
- Decomissioned in 1996, replaced by \acr{GPS}
:::

::: {.column}
![](assets/figures/Transit-o.jpg){height="500"}
:::

:::

### History of GPS

```{mermaid}
timeline
    title 🛰️ A Short History of GPS

    1973 : GPS program begins
         : The U.S. Department of Defense starts developing a global satellite navigation system.

    1978 : First GPS satellite
         : The first experimental GPS satellite is launched.

    1983 : GPS opened to civilians
         : The U.S. announces that GPS will eventually be available for civilian use.

    1995 : GPS becomes operational
         : The constellation reaches Full Operational Capability.
         : 🌍 Global positioning becomes a reality.

    2000 : Selective Availability switched off
         : Civilian GPS accuracy improves dramatically.
         : 📱 GPS begins its transition to mass-market technology.

    2010s : GPS becomes ubiquitous
          : Smartphones, vehicles, aviation, surveying and many other applications adopt GPS.

    Today : Part of the GNSS ecosystem
          : GPS operates alongside Galileo, GLONASS, BeiDou and other systems.
          : 🌐 Satellite positioning becomes global infrastructure.
```

### GNSS segments

To obtain a \acr{PVT}, we need:


::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment}
A way to compute the travel time
:::
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment}
A way to know the satellite location
:::
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment}
At least 4 satellites in view
:::
:::
:::


::: {.fragment}
::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
To satisfy these requirements, a GNSS system is composed of:

- **Space** segment: the satellites transmitting the positioning signals
- **Control** segment: the ground stations monitoring the satellites
- **User** segment: the receivers that compute their \acr{PVT}
:::

::: {.column}
![](assets/figures/gnss_system_overview.svg)
:::
:::
:::



### Space segment: overview

Contain the orbiting satellites that broadcast:
1. Navigation **signals** with synchronization patterns needed to compute the travel time
2. Navigation **message** with the satellite location and other information

| Space Segment | GPS | GLONASS | Galileo | BeiDou |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Num. orbital planes | 6 | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| Total num. satellites | 30 | 24 | 32 | 35 |
| Altitude (km) | 20,200 | 19,100 | 23,200 | 21,500 (MEO) |
| Inclination (°) | 55 | 64.8 | 56 | 55 |
| Orbital period (h) | 11.97 | 11.25 | 14.0 | 13.1 |

### Space segment: orbit types

![source: Wikipedia](assets/figures/orbit_types.svg)

### Space segment: multi-layer PNT

![source: ESA](assets/figures/multi_layer_PNT.png)

### Space segment: how to identify them?

A GNSS satellite is identified by these parameters:

::: {.incremental}
- **Constellation**: GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou, ...
- **SVN**: Space Vehicle Number, unique for each satellite in a constellation
- **PRN**: Pseudo-Random Noise code (identifies the signal), new satellites are assigned the next available PRN number (available upon satellite decommissioning)
:::

### Control segment


::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
- Composed of monitoring stations with known position
  - They resolve the *inverse* GNSS problem

- Continuous tasks:
  - Track status of satellites (monitoring stations)
  - Estimate satellite orbits and clock offsets (master control station)
  - Upload navigation messages to satellites (uplink stations)

- Less frequently
  - Send instructions for orbit keeping
  - Clock corrections
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}

![](assets/figures/gnss_segments_control.svg)

:::

:::

### Control segment: Galileo

![source: [EUSPA](https://www.gsc-europa.eu/system-service-status/ground-segment)](assets/figures/galileo_ground_stations.png)

### Control segment: Galileo

The Galileo ground segment is composed of:

- 2 \acr{GCC}: spacecraft housekeeping, constellation maintenance, navigation message and timing data determination
- 15 \acr{GSS}: collect \acr{SiS} measurements from GNSS satellites and forward them to the \acr{GCC}
- 5 \acr{ULS}: uplink navigation messages to the satellites

### Control segment: GPS

![source: [GPS.gov](https://archive.gps.gov/systems/gps/control/)](assets/figures/gps_ground_stations.png)

### Control segment: GPS
The GPS ground segment is composed of:

- \acr{MCS}: Controls the GPS constellation. Has an alternate (redundant) location
- Monitor stations: Tracking of the navigation signals of the satellites. Placed
strategically to maximize coverage.
- Ground antennas: Transmit control orders and the navigation message
generated by the \acr{MCS} to the satellites.

### User segment

Formed by all the set of GNSS receivers, classified as:

- Type of user:
  - Civilian: “not authorized” receivers. They are limited with respect the type of signals to be used, and then the performance of the service is lower
  - Military: Army and authorized organizations such as OTAN. They gave greater performance without any limitation of the service
- Frequency:
  - Single frequency: Track only one frequency band (L1 band)
  - Multi-frequency: Track different frequency bands (L1, L2 or L5). This is useful to mitigate ionospheric effects.
- Constellation capabilities (single, multi-constellation)
- Accuracy: can process carrier-phase? only code?
